title: Full-Spectrum Quantum Simulation for the Nuclear Shell Model
authors: B. Maheshwari, P. Stevenson, P. Van Isacker
abstract: The nuclear shell model is a general way of expressing the many-body nuclear Hamiltonian and deciphering the underlying nuclear structure. In today's era of modern and high-power computation, the primary limitation of the nuclear shell model is the enormous dimensionality of its Hilbert space, which far exceeds available storage capacity and prevents the diagonalization of the full Hamiltonian matrix in that space. Quantum computing offers a scalable solution to bypass this curse of dimensionality. In this work, we introduce a single-run quantum simulation capable of obtaining multiple shell-model eigenstates simultaneously. The nuclear Hamiltonian is transformed from a bit to a qubit basis using the Jordan-Wigner transformation, explicitly preserving fermionic anti-commutation. We employ a Subspace Search Variational Quantum Eigensolver (SSVQE) along with an Adaptive Derivative-Assembled Pseudo-Trotter (ADAPT) ansatz to construct the quantum circuit required to solve the shell-model problem. The ADAPT-SSVQE algorithm uses a symmetry-preserving single and double-excitation operator pool and optimizes a weighted energy sum to obtain the simultaneous convergence of all eigenstates within a targeted MJ subspace, eliminating the need for post-processing efforts to extract excited spectra. We benchmark this approach by solving the problem for two and three identical nucleons in a j = 9/2 orbital, successfully extracting five and ten mutually orthogonal states, respectively, within a 10-qubit active space. The algorithm achieves spectroscopic accuracy, in simulation, relative to exact diagonalization and intrinsically restores total angular momentum (\hat{J}^2) symmetry.
summary: This work presents a novel quantum simulation technique, ADAPT-SSVQE, designed to solve the intractable problem of diagonalizing large nuclear shell model Hamiltonians. By mapping the fermionic Hamiltonian to qubits and using an adaptive variational approach, the authors can simultaneously find multiple excited states for small nucleon systems with high accuracy. This demonstrates a powerful pathway toward simulating complex quantum many-body physics beyond classical computational limits.
main_problem: The primary challenge is overcoming the exponential dimensionality of the nuclear shell model Hamiltonian diagonalization, which exceeds classical computational capacity.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated a quantum simulation approach that simultaneously extracts multiple orthogonal eigenstates for two and three nucleons with spectroscopic accuracy relative to exact diagonalization.
method: They employ an ADAPT-SSVQE algorithm, combining the Subspace Search VQE with the ADAPT ansatz, applied after mapping the fermionic Hamiltonian using the Jordan-Wigner transformation.
model_or_system: The system is based on the nuclear shell model Hamiltonian ($\hat{H}_{	ext{eff}}$) describing protons and neutrons interacting via a residual interaction (e.g., JUN45). The problem is mapped onto qubits while preserving fermionic anti-commutation relations.
key_observables: Simultaneous convergence of multiple mutually orthogonal eigenstates, restoration of total angular momentum ($\hat{J}^2$) symmetry, and energy eigenvalues compared to exact diagonalization.
important_parameters: The simulation was benchmarked for two and three identical nucleons in a $j = 9/2$ orbital within a 10-qubit active space.
main_assumptions: The primary limitation addressed is the exponential scaling of the Hilbert space; the method assumes quantum computation can scale beyond classical limits, though circuit depth remains a concern for NISQ devices.
figures_summary: Figures track energy convergence and relative error over simulation iterations for two and three nucleons. They also show the growth of CNOT gate count, illustrating the increasing complexity of the required quantum circuits.
paper_structure: The paper details the theoretical framework by mapping the fermionic Hamiltonian to qubits (JW transformation). It then introduces and implements the ADAPT-SSVQE algorithm for simultaneous state extraction, culminating in benchmarking results for 2 and 3 nucleons showing convergence and symmetry restoration.
why_interesting: While focused on nuclear physics, the core methodology—using advanced quantum algorithms like ADAPT-SSVQE to tackle exponentially hard many-body problems while enforcing symmetries—is directly transferable to simulating strongly correlated electron systems or complex molecular Hamiltonians in AMO physics.
